#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA)
Description: The Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA) collects data for new residential construction. The SOMA reports provide information on amenities, rent/sales price levels, number of units, type of building, and the number of units taken off the market (absorbed). The data are collected at quarterly intervals until 12 months expire or until the units in a building are completely absorbed, which may occur sooner.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA)
Description: The Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA) collects data for new residential construction. The SOMA reports provide information on amenities, rent/sales price levels, number of units, type of building, and the number of units taken off the market (absorbed). The data are collected at quarterly intervals until 12 months expire or until the units in a building are completely absorbed, which may occur sooner.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I have strong initial results. Let me pull more detail from the Census history page and HUD User dataset page.One more round to fill in details on publications, sample design, and data access history.# Research Report: Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA)

## 1. Verification of Your Description

Your description is **accurate** — it matches nearly verbatim the official language used by both the U.S. Census Bureau and HUD User (HUD's Office of Policy Development and Research web portal). Minor refinements worth noting:

- SOMA covers buildings with **five or more units** (multifamily), a key scope limitation not explicit in your text.
- The "quarterly intervals" are structured as interviews at **3, 6, 9, and 12 months after completion** of the building.
- The survey focuses on **privately financed, nonsubsidized** units; units receiving federal subsidies (e.g., Section 8) are essentially out of scope for characteristics collection.

---

## 2. Who Publishes and Sponsors It

| Role | Entity |
|---|---|
| **Sponsor / funder** | U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R). HUD is the *sole* sponsor. |
| **Data collector / publisher** | U.S. Census Bureau (U.S. Department of Commerce), conducted on a reimbursable basis for HUD. Program contact: Financial and Market Characteristics Branch, census.soma@census.gov. |
| **Distribution portals** | census.gov (reports and tables), the Census Data API (`api.census.gov/data/timeseries/soma`), data.census.gov, HUD User (huduser.gov/portal/datasets/soma), and catalog.data.gov. |

The Data.gov catalog entry (identifier `SOMATIMESERIES`) lists the dataset as public, U.S. coverage, temporal span 2014–present in the API, licensed CC0/public domain.

## 3. Legal Authority and Administrative Mandate

- **Authorizing statute:** 12 U.S.C. §§ 1701z-1 and 1701z-2 — HUD's research and survey authority, originating in the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1970 (cited in OMB filings as the "United States Housing Act of 1970"). This authorizes HUD to conduct research on housing markets; Census conducts the fieldwork under its general statistical authority.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** OMB Control Number **2528-0013**, titled "Survey of Market Absorption of New Apartment Buildings." The most recent renewal (April 2024) is active with an expiration of **September 30, 2026**, and a further extension notice was published in the Federal Register in July 2026. Current inventory: ~48,000 responses and ~6,000 burden hours annually (up to four ~20-minute interviews per sampled building; respondents are rental agents, builders, and property managers).
- **Confidentiality:** Responses are protected under **Title 13, U.S.C.**; only aggregate tabulations are released. There is **no public-use microdata file** — an important fact for data scientists and preservationists alike.
- **Records disposition:** NARA records schedule DAA-0029-2013-0001 (2013) covers SOMA public documentation, including questionnaires, glossaries, quarterly/annual reports, and data tables designated for permanent transfer.

## 4. History

- **1970:** The survey began; it has run continuously for over five decades, making it one of the longest-running federal housing market indicators.
- **Publication lineage:** Data were long issued in the *Current Housing Reports* series — **H-130, "Market Absorption of Apartments"** (quarterly + annual) and **H-131, "Characteristics of Apartments Completed"** (annual). PDF scans of H-130 reports back to the 1970s are available in the Census Library; historical issues were distributed through the Federal Depository Library Program (FDLP; e.g., PURL purl.fdlp.gov/GPO/LPS56308).
- **1990–91:** Estimation procedure modified — separate ratio-estimate factors computed for each of the four census regions rather than one national factor (a comparability caveat for long time series).
- **2001:** The parent Survey of Construction revised its methodology for estimating 5+ unit completions; Census cautions against comparing SOMA data across that break without care.
- **2002:** Began collecting data on **"Senior Housing"** and assisted-living-type units.
- **~2014:** Data made available through the Census Data API as a time series.
- **Present:** Fully internet-disseminated; quarterly releases the first week of March, June, September, and December, with pre-publication tables roughly one month earlier, the H-130 Annual in early April, and the H-131 Characteristics report in early July. Every five years a comprehensive historical report with additional tables is produced.

## 5. Methodology (for Data Scientists)

- **Sampling frame:** The Census Bureau's **Survey of Construction (SOC)**. The SOC divides the U.S. into primary sampling units stratified by population and permit activity; all new 5+ unit buildings in sampled permit-issuing places are included.
- **Coverage limitation:** Only **permit-issuing areas** (~98% of 5+ unit construction). Non-permit areas are excluded.
- **Sample size:** Roughly **4,000–4,100 buildings per year** (quarterly samples of ~800–1,200 buildings). Weighted response rates are exceptionally high, ~**99%**.
- **Interview design:** A building is interviewed 3 months after completion; if not fully absorbed, re-interviewed at 6, 9, and 12 months. The interview ends when units are fully absorbed, 12 months elapse, or subsidized status is discovered.
- **Unit types:** Unfurnished rental apartments (the core series), furnished rentals, condominiums, cooperatives, and senior housing (2002+). Excluded: subsidized/PHA-owned units, time-shares, dormitories, townhouses sold individually, group quarters, continuing-care facilities.
- **Variables:** Number of units, bedrooms, asking rent / sales price, absorption counts and rates at 3/6/9/12 months, building type, amenities (air conditioning, swimming pools, etc.), furnished status, senior housing services.
- **Estimation:** Base weights (inverse probability of selection) with regional ratio adjustment to SOC completion totals; annual rates are weighted averages of quarterly estimates. **Standard errors and margins of error are published** in annual Source and Accuracy statements (available as PDFs in the technical documentation directory at www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/soma/technical-documentation/).
- **Geography:** National, four census regions (and divisions), inside/outside metropolitan areas historically, plus absorption rates for **selected large metropolitan areas** (those with sufficient permit activity).
- **API:** `api.census.gov/data/timeseries/soma` — requires a free API key; supports quarterly and annual estimates with margins of error, by unit type and characteristics. Tables also downloadable as XLS/CSV/PDF.

## 6. Typical Users

Documented users include:

- **HUD/PD&R** — assessing rental market tightness, housing supply adequacy, and whether multifamily construction meets public need.
- **The Federal Reserve Board** — comparing asking rents on new rental properties with monthly mortgage payment data (explicitly cited in the PRA supporting statement).
- **Builders and developers** — gauging demand and lease-up risk for new projects.
- **Banks and lenders** — underwriting multifamily construction loans.
- **Market analysts and real estate economists** — absorption rates as a barometer of demand.
- **Land planners and local governments** — measuring need for federal, state, and local housing assistance.
- **Academics and housing researchers** — long-run studies of rental markets, condominium conversion, and senior housing supply.

## 7. Benefits to the Public

- **Unique indicator:** SOMA is essentially the only federal statistical series measuring *how fast* new multifamily supply is absorbed — a direct, nationally consistent measure of rental/condo market tightness that private data vendors do not replicate with the same methodology or history.
- **50+ year time series** enabling analysis across multiple housing cycles (the 1973 peak of 531,700 unfurnished rental completions; the post-2008 trough; the 2010s apartment boom).
- **Transparency and market efficiency:** free, public-domain data reduce information asymmetry for small builders, local governments, and advocates.
- **Policy input:** informs debates over housing supply adequacy, affordability, and senior housing, complementing HUD's other sponsored series (American Housing Survey, Survey of Construction, Manufactured Housing Survey, Rental Housing Finance Survey).

## 8. Notes for Preservationists and Data Librarians

- **What exists:** (a) scanned historical H-130/H-131 PDFs in the Census Library (census.gov/library) and FDLP collections; (b) current quarterly/annual tables in XLS/CSV/PDF at census.gov/programs-surveys/soma; (c) the API time series (2014 forward in the API, though tables cover earlier years); (d) technical documentation including annual Source & Accuracy statements; (e) NARA-scheduled permanent public documentation.
- **What does *not* exist publicly:** respondent-level microdata — absorption data survive only as published aggregates, so **preserving the published tables is the only way to preserve the data series itself**.
- **Format risks:** API is the primary machine-readable channel and requires a key; the web table interface has been reorganized multiple times (legacy URL census.gov/housing/soma now redirects). The HUD User mirror is bot-protected and an unreliable archival target.
- **Programmatic risk:** SOMA is a small, **reimbursable interagency program** wholly dependent on HUD PD&R funding — the category of survey most vulnerable to budget cuts or discontinuation. Its OMB clearance must be renewed (currently expiring September 2026), and each renewal is a point at which the survey could be altered or terminated. The Data.gov entry's "last updated" date (September 2023) also suggests stale catalog metadata.
- **Recommended preservation actions:** mirror the full XLS/CSV table archive and the Source & Accuracy PDFs; capture H-130/H-131 PDFs (1970s–present) from the Census Library and FDLP PURLs; archive the API variable/geography documentation; snapshot the every-five-years comprehensive historical reports, which are the richest consolidated source.

## Key Sources

- Census Bureau SOMA program pages: census.gov/programs-surveys/soma (about, data, library, FAQ, history)
- Census SOMA history page (census.gov/about/history/...)
- Census API documentation: census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/soma.html
- OMB/reginfo ICR 2528-0013 (202404-2528-003) and 2017 PRA Supporting Statement (omb.report)
- Federal Register notices (2004, 2020, 2026) on SOMA information collection
- NARA records schedule DAA-0029-2013-0001
- H-130 Annual 2016 report (h130-16A.pdf) for methodology, sample sizes, and response rates
- Data.gov catalog entry: catalog.data.gov/dataset/survey-of-market-absorption
- HUD User SOMA dataset page and PD&R Edge article "The Evolution of Housing Data in the United States, Part 2"

I'll research the current risk context for SOMA — recent Federal Register activity, Census Bureau and HUD PD&R staffing/funding changes, and any administration actions affecting federal statistical programs.Key findings so far — including a notable September 2025 HUD Request for Information on the uses of SOMA data. Let me dig deeper into that RFI, HUD PD&R staffing, and publication continuity.I now have enough evidence to complete the assessment. Note: the USAJobs tracker was archived on December 31, 2025 and its data loads via JavaScript, so I could not extract agency figures from it directly; I rely instead on GAO, ASA/American Statistical Association, OMB, Federal Register, and budget documents.

---

# Risk Assessment: Survey of Market Absorption of New Multifamily Units (SOMA)
**Assessment date: October 2026**

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue:* The Census Bureau's online library continues to host scanned H-130/H-131 reports back to the 1970s; current quarterly/annual tables (XLS/CSV/PDF) and the API time series remain posted; the SOMA data page was last updated May 12, 2026. No removals of prior-year files were found. A NARA records schedule (DAA-0029-2013-0001) designates SOMA public documentation for permanent retention.
- *Moderate/High:* No evidence of removed data elements or files. (Caveats outside the rubric: Data.gov catalog metadata is stale — "last updated" 2023 — and no public microdata has ever existed, so the published tables are the only record.)

**Determination: No Known Issue.** Prior-cycle data remain accessible with no known alterations.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue:* HUD ran the full PRA renewal cycle on schedule — 60-day notice March 2, 2026 (91 FR 10104), 30-day notice July 23, 2026 (91 FR 46449), ICR submitted to OIRA July 23, 2026 as an "extension without change" (reginfo 202606-2528-001). HUD's FY2026 Congressional Justification explicitly lists SOMA among the surveys Core R&T funding supports. Collection and quarterly publication continued through at least mid-2026.
- *Moderate Risk:* The prior ICR approval **expired September 30, 2026**, and as of this assessment the renewal remains in "Received in OIRA" status — i.e., the ICR is technically lapsed (less than one year → Moderate). Additionally, the October–November 2025 government shutdown furloughed most Census staff and disrupted release schedules across the Bureau (Census Project, Nov 2025), and ~100 Census employees received RIF notices during the shutdown.
- *High Risk:* Would apply if the ICR lapse exceeds one year or a publication cycle is skipped — not currently the case.

**Determination: Moderate Risk.** Renewal was properly initiated and HUD clearly intends to continue the survey, but the ICR has just expired with OIRA review pending, and shutdown-related disruption already occurred. If OIRA approves the pending ICR, this would revert toward No Known Issue.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- *No Known Issue:* The 2026 ICR is an "extension without change" — identical 48,000 responses, 6,000 burden hours, same instrument (HUD Form SOMA). No announced reductions in granularity, geography, or frequency.
- *Moderate Risk:* Emerging capacity risks: the Census Bureau lost an estimated 15–20% of staff between FY2024 and FY2026 (ASA "Nation's Data at Risk"; GovExec, Aug 2026), and the Commerce IG has documented chronic field representative vacancies — field reps are exactly who conduct SOMA's 3/6/9/12-month interviews. HUD PD&R, which sponsors and oversees the survey, was "singled out for particularly large staffing cuts" (Shelterforce tracker; NPR). HUD's September 2025 RFI explicitly invited comments on "included or missing content in the SOMA," opening the door to content changes.
- *High Risk:* No actual reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency have been documented.

**Determination: Moderate Risk.** Quality is currently maintained, but staffing erosion at both the collecting and sponsoring agencies, plus an open-ended content review, present credible emerging risk.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- *High Risk:* SOMA rests only on HUD's general research authority (12 U.S.C. §§ 1701z-1, 1701z-2; OMB filings cite the Housing and Urban Development Act of 1970). The survey is **not named in any statute**, has **no statutory publication deadline**, and — unlike PD&R's fair market rents or income limits — is **not required to implement any federal program**. It is a discretionary, reimbursable interagency program wholly dependent on annual PD&R funding decisions. Commercial substitutes (CoStar, RealPage, Moody's/REIS) exist, though they are proprietary and methodologically different.
- *Moderate Risk:* Would require that SOMA be needed to implement a federal program — it is not, directly.
- Mitigating: HUD's own FY2026 budget documents call SOMA part of "the backbone of the Nation's housing data infrastructure," and the Federal Reserve and lenders use it; but this is programmatic value, not statutory mandate.

**Determination: High Risk.** The rubric's High tier is triggered squarely: authorization is vague/general, there is no statutory collection or publication requirement, and there is no legally protected programmatic use — which is also exactly why the program could be evaluated for termination via a simple RFI (see Policy).

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- *High Risk:* Multiple High-tier criteria are met:
  - **Leadership removed:** Census Director Robert Santos resigned under pressure in February 2025; the Bureau ran on acting leadership (including a political appointee, George Cook, named acting director September 2025) until Brett Matsumoto's confirmation in 2026 (ASA; GovExec).
  - **Budget cut ≥20% proposed:** The FY2026 President's Budget proposed **$95M for PD&R's Research & Technology account — a ~20–22% cut** from the $119M FY2025 enacted level (NLIHC analysis; HUD FY2026 CJ). SOMA is funded from this account. (Final FY2026 enacted level could not be confirmed in available sources; appropriations were disrupted by a partial shutdown.)
  - **Staff losses:** Census lost ~15–20% of staff FY2024→FY2026 (ASA; GovExec). HUD's FY2026 budget assumes ~1,750 fewer staff than end-2024 (~21% HUD-wide), and a September 2026 HUD reorganization notice states staffing is "almost 35 percent below historic staffing levels." PD&R specifically was targeted for outsized cuts (NPR; Shelterforce).
- *Moderate Risk:* If one counted only confirmed/enacted figures and excluded leadership, the Census (~15–20%) and HUD (~21%) staff losses fall in the 10–39% band → Moderate. But leadership removal and the proposed ≥20% budget cut independently satisfy High-tier criteria.

**Determination: High Risk.** Leadership removal at the collecting agency, a proposed ≥20% cut to the sponsoring account, and double-digit staff losses at both agencies — with the sponsoring office specifically targeted.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- *Moderate Risk:* On **September 9, 2025**, HUD published a **Request for Information on the Uses of SOMA Data** (90 FR 43468), stating it "is evaluating current needs for data from the Survey of Market Absorption" and soliciting comment on uses and content, signed by John Gibbs, Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for PD&R — a political appointee — amid the administration's DOGE/ARRP efficiency drive. The comment period was extended to January 30, 2026 (90 FR, Dec. 16, 2025). An agency publicly questioning whether it still needs a dataset it sponsors is a clear "change being considered or planned" signal.
- *High Risk:* Would require an actual Presidential Action-driven ICR, a negative policy notice on the site, or implemented changes. None occurred — importantly, HUD's subsequent action (March–July 2026) was to seek **extension without change**, and no content alterations or anti-data messaging have appeared on the SOMA pages.
- *No Known Issue:* Not supportable, given the RFI.

**Determination: Moderate Risk.** The administration formally opened an evaluation of whether SOMA data are still needed — a pending-consideration posture — but as of this assessment has acted to continue the survey unchanged.

**Overall interpretation:** SOMA is currently alive and publishing, with a renewal ICR pending and its sponsor's own budget documents endorsing it. However, its structural vulnerability is severe: it is a small, discretionary, reimbursable program with only general statutory authority, sponsored by an office (PD&R) that was explicitly targeted for deep cuts under a proposed ~20% budget reduction, collected by an agency that has lost up to a fifth of its staff and its Senate-confirmed leadership, and it has already been the subject of an administration RFI questioning the need for its data. The single most important near-term watch item is OIRA's disposition of ICR 202606-2528-001 (expired September 30, 2026) — prolonged inaction would push Future Data Availability toward High Risk.
